title: From a scalar identity to Mathlib's Pell group
content: The parent entry proves the scalar identity `(x²+2y²)² − 2(2xy)² = 1` for every solution of `x² − 2y² = −1`, but that statement lives entirely in `ℤ` and never touches Mathlib's group-theoretic model `Pell.Solution₁`. This file *promotes* the bridge into `Pell.Solution₁ 2`, organising everything around the coset structure of the unit group of `ℤ√2`: the norm `+1` solutions are an index-2 subgroup and the norm `−1` solutions are the nontrivial coset — the 'other half'. The fundamental unit `1+√2` has norm `−1`; its square `3+2√2` generates the norm `+1` solutions.
mathContext: Unit group of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ (mod $\pm1$) is generated by $1+\sqrt2$ (norm $-1$); $\texttt{Pell.Solution}_1\,2$ is the norm $+1$ subgroup.

title: Brahmagupta composition for d = 2
content: `negMul_norm` is Brahmagupta's identity specialized to `d = 2`: the product of two norm `−1` solutions satisfies the norm `+1` Pell equation. The proof is a single `ring` rewrite of the left side into `(x₁²−2y₁²)(x₂²−2y₂²)`, then substituting the two hypotheses and computing `(−1)·(−1) = 1`. This is the multiplicativity of the `ℤ√2`-norm made completely elementary.

title: The promotion is honest ℤ√2 multiplication
content: `negMul` promotes the scalar product into `Pell.Solution₁ 2` via `Solution₁.mk`, but the mathematically important lemma is `coe_negMul`: the promoted element's underlying `ℤ√2` value is *literally* the ring product `⟨x₁,y₁⟩ · ⟨x₂,y₂⟩`. This is what makes the construction genuine rather than an ad-hoc coordinate formula — it is proved by unfolding `mk`, rewriting with `coe_mk`, and matching components via the `Zsqrtd` multiplication simp lemmas `re_mul`/`im_mul`. The `@[simp]` component lemmas `negMul_x`/`negMul_y` are pure `rfl`.

title: The squaring bridge as the diagonal
content: `negSquare` is defined as the diagonal `negMul x y x y` — squaring is just composition of a solution with itself, which is why `(−1)·(−1)=+1` makes it land in `Pell.Solution₁ 2`. `coe_negSquare` then identifies the promoted square with `⟨x,y⟩²` in `ℤ√2`, giving the precise sense in which the parent's scalar `negPell_sq_is_pos_pell` *is* squaring inside Mathlib's model. `negSquare_one_one` records the fundamental instance: `(1,1)` squares to the fundamental Pell solution `(3,2)`.

title: Coset closure: the negatives are half the unit group
content: `posMul_neg_norm` is the structural payoff: multiplying a positive Pell solution `a ∈ Solution₁ 2` by a negative solution stays in the negative class, because the norm is a homomorphism and `(+1)·(−1) = −1`. Together with `negMul` (which shows `(−1)·(−1) = +1` returns to the subgroup), this exhibits the norm `−1` solutions as a single coset of the norm `+1` subgroup — the 'other half' of the unit group of `ℤ√2`.
mathContext: Norm homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]^\times\to\{\pm1\}$: kernel = norm $+1$ (Solution₁), nontrivial coset = norm $-1$.
